newsitem.title: USA: Sharpton seen livening up NYC mayor race.
newsitem.headline: Sharpton seen livening up NYC mayor race.

text.p: The entry of controversial activist Al Sharpton into next year's race for New York City mayor is likely to put a jolt into a campaign many have seen as ho-hum so far.

While few give Sharpton any chance of defeating Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, the flamboyant black minister could emerge in the enviable position of powerbroker, political analysts said. Sharpton declared his candidacy Sunday without saying whether he will run as a Democrat or an independent.

A strong showing in the Democratic primary could give him clout to help determine who faces Giuliani, a moderate Republican, in the general election. An independent run by Sharpton could siphon off enough traditional Democratic black votes to guarantee Giuliani's re-election, analysts said.
Giuliani was elected in 1993, the first Republican to hold the mayor's office in a generation. The former federal prosecutor defeated David Dinkins, the city's first black mayor, by a slim margin.
"Sharpton will make it a lot more interesting than it was going to be," said Michael Tomasky, a political columnist at New York magazine.
"He definitely shakes things up," said Democratic pollster Chris Lapetina of Global Strategy Group. "He'll get more press attention than anybody else and he's not scared to attack."
Polls have shown Giuliani defeating all of the oft-mentioned challengers if the election were held now.

Among his likely Democratic challengers, none well-known outside the city, are Manhattan Borough President Ruth Messinger, Bronx Borough President Fernando Ferrer, City Comptroller Alan Hevesi and Brooklyn City Councilman Sal Albanese, the first to toss his hat officially into the ring.

If Sharpton, the only black among them, runs in the party primary he could strike deals with the winner in exchange for his support, Tomasky said. But a Democrat seen as beholden to Sharpton could lose more moderate votes to Giuliani and boost the mayor's chances considerably, he said.
"He'll have a heavy card to play, which in the end probably means the Democrats have less of a chance to beat Giuliani," Tomasky said.
"There will be people who might want to vote for a Democratic candidate but who will fear the influence of Sharpton," former Mayor Ed Koch said.

Sharpton made an unexpectedly strong showing in 1992 in a four-way Democratic Senate primary, finishing ahead of former City Controller Elizabeth Holtzman. He was seen as having shed his more controversial image to become a credible candidate.

But the ghosts of Sharpton's past will haunt him, political analysts agree, particularly his role as adviser to Tawana Brawley, a black teenager who in 1987 was found nude and covered with excrement in upstate New York. With Sharpton at her side, Brawley claimed several white men kidnapped and raped her, but the claim proved to be a hoax.
"He's made an effort to redefine himself but a lot of people are stuck with that old image," Lapetina said. "That's his Chappaquiddick."

While no challenger has emerged as an overwhelming threat, Giuliani is vulnerable, analysts say. Admired as tenacious and independent, he has overseen a drop in crime and designed a working city budget, but his heavy-handed style has forced out several popular city figures including Police Commisioner William Bratton and Schools Chancellor Ramon Cortines and has led many to accuse him of behaving like a schoolyard bully.

"People don't like Giuliani in this town," said John Mollenkopf, a professor of political science at the City University of New York. "People feel for all the good he's done ... he beats up on everyone who disagrees with him."
To keep his job, Giuliani must retain the coalition that elected him -- the city's few Republicans and the disgruntled Democrats who voiced unhappiness with the ineffective Dinkins.
"It's still a Democratic town," Lapetina said. "If someone can come up with why voters should get rid of Giuliani, I think people will respond."
